summary:
Argentina's statutory framework remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was also the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws. A visitor to this province stands under that framework.

The framework has been narrowed by executive action. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention; no outcome of that challenge is sourced here.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a ten-year record and a 62% increase year on year, averaging one every 38 hours. Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space, with beatings the main modality. Institutional violence rose to 64 cases in 2025, compared with 17 in 2024, and 32% of 2025 incidents took place in police stations or prisons. Contact with the security forces is therefore the single most consequential exposure a trans visitor faces, and 43% of perpetrators were strangers to their victims.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

No trans-specific provincial statute, enforcement series or incident pattern was documented for this province, and the province has no local reporting infrastructure capable of generating separate records. Absence of documentation here indicates no evidence gathered, not an absence of exposure.
tangentialFactors:
Activists interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán and for the activist Lohana Berkins, described the Milei government's policies as having made the community more vulnerable to violence and the situation as chaotic and desperate. Agencia Presentes described the 2025 hate-crime total as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm.

Police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has worsened since President Milei took office and is reported as worst outside Buenos Aires, in the more conservative interior provinces. Agencia Presentes and the Washington Blade place the national picture in that pattern, in which security-force personnel account for a large share of recorded perpetrators.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, with an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position. The contrast with the 2012 statute, described by the United Nations as pioneering, and with the 2010 marriage-equality law is the comparison that frames Argentina's current standing.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same February 2025 decree that restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and the accompanying decree on the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and indicated an intention to seek judicial intervention.

Transgender people hired under the 1% Trans Labor Quota were dismissed, and the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI was abolished, according to activists quoted by the Washington Blade in April 2025. These are resident-facing losses of both employment protection and a complaint channel.

The province retains local petty-offence police codes identified by an NGO survey as the instrument behind most arrests of trans and travesti people, which is the mechanism through which ordinary policing converts into recorded institutional violence.

Because the province has no local reporting infrastructure, incidents occurring here are absorbed into national totals rather than generating provincial figures, so residents have no provincial count to consult.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the legal challenge to the February 2025 decrees succeeded, failed or remains pending is unresolved in the sources available; only the intention to seek judicial intervention is documented.

The dismissal of 1% Trans Labor Quota workers and the abolition of INADI are sourced to activist testimony reported in April 2025 rather than to an official announcement or publication in the sources supplied, and the precise legal form of the abolition is not sourced.

Whether this province falls inside or outside the pattern in which police violence against trans and travesti sex workers is reported as worst is unresolved; the sources describe the interior-province pattern nationally and do not disaggregate it to this province.

No local incident series, arrest record or provincial statute specific to this province was found in the available material, which indicates no documentation rather than no exposure, and the national hate-crime totals are not broken down by province.
